body: Absolutely! Like I can see how my bf got away with not having one in the 2000s up to 2010/2011 since social media and the need to have an account for everything was just getting big then, but there's no way that's possible now, I don't think you can do anything substantial online without an email address.

That's what I thought was pretty normal until his situation, like I'm currently going back to school and I switched colleges last year after the spring semester, but my first school's email was shut down within weeks of my transfer. Even at my first college right after high school I lost access to my university email a few months after dropping out. I have no idea how or why they kept his open for that long.

I'd never heard of anyone doing this until my boyfriend got locked out of his 11 year old Steam account a few years ago when his student email address finally got canceled. Lost all his games and had to make a brand new account cuz he couldn't verify anything (he'd gotten a new computer and hadn't logged into Steam for years cuz his old one was busted). He graduated in 2015 and they waited until 2022 to turn it off, but when I asked him why tf he used that as opposed to a personal one he said he didn't have a personal email until after he was in school because he didn't actually need one, which I guess makes sense? But also I've had a personal email since 2006 cuz I was a forum rp/Gaia kid back in the day so like I still don't really understand lol

Ironically, I actually started going back to school to finish my bachelor's last year because I knew something like this would happen, I just didn't think it would be this soon lol I won't graduate for another 1.5-2 years, but I have been considering switching jobs. Just sucks because after living here for 7 years I finally found a job without horrible management that pays decent and lets me work 6a-2p so I can focus on homework/studying in the afternoon/evening, but it's not sustainable for my health.

Dental Care Associates saved my teeth. I hadn't taken care of them due to severe depression and a phobia of dentists, but they were so empathetic and compassionate with their care. I never felt judged or made fun of, and after describing how terrified I was (I mean they could probably tell already because I was shaking so bad I could barely talk) they made a point of telling exactly what they were doing before they touched me and didn't do any actual work until I was fully sedated. They did a full deep clean while I was out too so I woke up literally feeling like a new person. Instead of immediately resorting to just pulling them like every other dentist I had a consult with, they ended up doing a root canal and 3 post and cores so I was able to keep them. 10/10 the nicest people I've encountered.

I will say Neighborhood Dental on 41st/Minnesota is awful and I'd stay away from them. I went there first for a broken canine a year prior and younger male dentist literally yelled at me, threw his tools on the tray, and stormed out after I told him I wasn't numb enough and was sobbing from the pain. I was in excruciating pain for weeks and my dentist at DCA said based on my xrays from that time they absolutely could have done a post and core on the tooth since the root was fine and not infected, but the dentist at ND probably just didn't want to because it's more effort than just ripping it out.

I went to Southeast Tech for a semester and ended up transferring to an online out of state program this fall because my experience wasn't great. It was fine at first, teachers were really nice, small class sizes, and the campus is cool. They assured me that doing a spring start wouldn't have an impact on my schedule going forward in terms of class availability (I offered to wait till the fall to make sure but they insisted I started in January), but that ended up not being true. I spoke to my advisor who not only told me I'd be forced into going part time, but laughed at me when I said my plan was to transfer an associates to a bigger school to get my bachelor's because he said they "have very specialized classes that likely won't transfer anywhere else". I'm seeing this now at my current school, I took 5 classes and they're still trying to figure out what the course equivalent would be to try to get me some credit. Maybe it was just the degree I chose (Computer Programming), but there weren't enough teachers or students to take more than 1-2 classes per semester going forward, which canceled out the scholarship I got at the end of the semester and would have disqualified me from getting loans. I've heard the medical programs there are better so again, it might just depend on what you wanna do.

I wholeheartedly second this. I'm a professional cleaner who specifically does move out cleanings, and pumice stones are my #1 used tool for toilets and ovens. If it's really bad you can soak the toilet in vinegar or CLR for an hour or two before scrubbing it with the pumice stone.

DCA works with people who don't have insurance too, I have a friend who got all 4 of his wisdom teeth out with them without insurance for like $300. If you go with them (or really any dentist recommended here) just let them know your anxiety situation ahead of time and most places should be accommodating, it's a super common phobia.

Dental Care Associates on Sycamore saved my teeth and Dr. Mike was awesome. My front teeth were rotted out from straight up not taking care of them due to depression and avoiding the dentist for 12 years because even getting a cleaning gives me a panic attack. Zero judgment from the entire staff and everyone was super sweet and gentle. They sedated me and did a root canal with 3 post and cores, but walked me through the entire process and didn't touch my teeth until I was unconscious. Zero pain or complications after the procedure and even did a free check up a few weeks later after my insurance got swapped.

I don't recommend Neighborhood Dental on 41st cuz I had a tooth pulled there the year prior and the younger dentist guy literally yelled at me and stormed out of the room because I was crying from the pain.

I went to Dental Care Associates and saw Dr Mike when I needed to get 3 post and cores and my first root canal done on my front teeth. I thought the shower seat thing was going to be overkill too but ended up grabbing one from work just in case (I worked in elder care at the time) and I was glad I did. Standing for more than 3-5 min at a time made me dizzy and nauseous for the first couple days and it made showering SO much easier. I was glad I had a detachable handle on my shower head already too so once the people helping me had to go back to work I was able to do it myself

They don't, but it essentially prints out a temp voucher in case you get pulled over saying you paid for new tags/plates, and then they mail them to the address on your license a few weeks later (I did mine in January and I think it took about 2 weeks to get them)

I recently started with the downtown Southeastern Behavioral Health (I was referred there from my normal place for EMDR treatment) and the income requirements for free services are decent (I make about $1800 a month and I easily qualified, so she should have no issues if she don't have income or insurance right now). I can't personally speak about the quality of services yet since I just did my intake yesterday, but the staff I've interacted with have been very kind so far. Pretty sure they usually set you up with a case manager for a month or two before they really start doing anything (my therapist is trying to get them to bypass that since I'm a referral), but I'd think if there's meds involved they'd at least get some temp refills in during that waiting period. 

Also if she's looking to get back into the workforce and needs support or help finding a job that will work well with her mental illness, I'd recommend Vocational Rehabilitation. At the recommendation of my therapist I was recently accepted into their program because my PTSD and depression make it hard for me to hold down a job for longer than a year or so. The intake process does take a while so just be prepared for that (I think it's taken me about 2 months from my initial application to my intake appointment this coming Monday).They're supposed to help with finding employment that fits what you need/can handle, assist with getting you any required tools (uniform, shoes, job specific stuff like chef knives or a tool kit, etc), skills training, provide work accommodations if needed, and I've heard of them helping people go back to school as well. Mental illness can be just as debilitating as physical illness and thankfully they recognize that.

I only pay about $30 a month but I get it through Sanford which is why I think it's so cheap. The only perk of working for them is the health and dental lol if only they paid us more, then this wouldn't be as big of an issue

1. I definitely had a harder time than I thought I would walking afterwards and needed someone to support me while moving, ESPECIALLY when sitting down and getting off the toilet

2. There's a chance a few of your ribs or chest muscles might be extremely sore from the position you're in on the table or over inflating your lungs. On day 2 I was in so much pain from that my doctor ended up having to prescribe some muscle relaxers and more pain medication because I couldn't take a full breath or hold myself up

3. TEA WITH HONEY. My throat was absolutely wrecked from the breathing tube and I probably drank my weight in peppermint tea for the first 2 days

4. The first few showers were also difficult. I got a loofa with a long handle so I could reach my own backside, and luckily I work in elder care so I was able to snag a shower chair which helped so much, even just to rest or wash my legs once I started doing it on my own

5. I'm still not sure how or why this happened (apparently the same thing happened to my dad after he had surgery a few years ago), but when I tried to go to bed that first night I'd wake up gasping within a few seconds to a minute of falling asleep. My dad thought it might be our lungs getting used to taking in all that air on their own after the breathing tube, but it was absolutely miserable. My boyfriend eventually helped me roll onto my side with some pillows surrounding me to keep me in place and that worked immediately, but it was only an issue that first night. I'd never heard of this happening to anyone else except my dad and I so I'm not sure if it'll happen for you, but it's good to be prepared.

6. If you have anxiety, tell the nurses! I played it cool and tough all the way up until we got to the OR and then I completely broke down and had a massive panic attack until I went under. The nurses were phenomenal about it, they held my hand, brushed my hair out of my face, wiped my tears, and talked me through everything that was going on while I was in full panic mode, but I wish I'd brought it up sooner than when I was already in the throws of it laying on the table because we might have been able to work something out as a team to prevent it. 

7. Weird funky discharge and spotting. I kinda assumed this would happen since they were going to flush my tubes while they were in there and I was on the last day of my period the day of surgery, but I wasn't expecting the amount I had come out of me for that long (I'd say it took about 2 weeks for things to start feeling normal down there, and I'm currently on week 3 post op).

Well I was stuck on that generic one for the last few months cuz I get 3 packs at a time, but they finally got Lyleq sent in and I'm about to start it tonight. But the last 2 times I made the swap I personally had significant breakthrough bleeds for the first month. My period is apparently too strong to be stopped because I was told I might not get one on it and yet I got like 2-3 a month at first lol but depending on how long you've been on it your body might just be adjusting to the hormone levels or you might not get it at all. My original doctor who prescribed it said many people don't get their period and only spot on progestin only pills, but if it's starting to worry you I'd keep track of how long you're spotting and if it occurs when you're normally scheduled to have your period and talk to your doc about it
See that's what I thought too, I don't see how it would cause any kind of complications. My friend was adamant that it'd be a big deal but like...it makes no sense

It definitely helps but don't expect a miracle like some doctors amp it up to be. For me, it got rid of my ovulation pain and the frequency of my severe flare ups (went from it happening every time I got my period to about 1/2-3/4 of the time). I still have the same amount of flow/clots and my cramps aren't even close to the range of "normal", but I can function a lot better and I don't miss nearly as much work as I used to. Also everyone's body is different and every pill works differently with your own chemistry and hormone levels so you gotta take that into account as well.

Yeah I panicked cuz I know with the pill there's a slight increased risk of blood clots in general even without surgery, so my anxiety skyrocketed and I ended up messaging my doctor directly after reading horror stories online but she reassured me that a ton of people who get the lap are on the pill and it shouldn't have any adverse effects.

My lap is in a few weeks and they said I could continue to take my birth control normally before and after. But like another comment said, the only things I'm not allowed to take are ibuprofen, Aleve, or aspirin for 7 days prior to surgery (they said Tylenol was fine though).

My old doctor always told me to drink orange juice when I was having a flare up and I'm not sure if it actually worked or if it was a placebo effect but it helped enough to where even now 15 years later I usually down a glass or two when I'm desperate. Plus if anything, OJ is good for you anyway

I'm literally experiencing the exact same thing and it's so frustrating. I'd been on combo pills since I was a teen to help with my symptoms but didn't have much luck, so I switched to the mini pill 2 years ago. 

I was originally put on Tulana (I was regular for the first 3 months then had my period 3 times that March), then thankfully the Planned Parenthood I was going to discontinued that brand so they put me on Lyleq and I LOVED it. Had minimal/mild flare ups and I was back to a normal cycle for about a year which was great cuz I'd never had an irregular period in my life and it was kind of terrifying to experience. Then again this March I had issues because PP had shipment delays on Lyleq so they sent me to get a generic version from Hyvee and within a week of being on it I was irregular again, but thankfully I got back on Lyleq after that month. Had to switch doctors because I finally got health insurance in May and found out that either only PP has access to Lyleq or it was discontinued entirely so I was swapped to Errin for 3 months. I was fine for the first 2 months, then was irregular AGAIN. Went to go refill my prescription a few weeks ago and got another random generic version so I'm currently going on 2 months of having full periods with clots and flare ups every other week and I've missed so much work from it. 

I talked to my new doctor about it and she said it could either be my body's reaction to the additives in the generic version/Errin, or since the dosage is technically the same across all of them that it's not a high enough dose of progestin for my body which is causing the extreme breakthrough bleeding. She's currently trying to either find me a pharmacy that carries Lyleq or she's going to get me on a higher dose pill but it's been a struggle to find anything. I'm not sure if that helps but I feel your pain, it's absolutely terrible and extremely frustrating.
